pr_title: `ec.h`: Explain use of `strstr()` for `EVP_EC_gen()` and add `#include <string.h>`
pr_body:
Fixes #17362

This should be done also for 3.0 because, as reported there, compilation fails in certain environments.

When porting a program to openssl, compilation failed because EVP_EC_gen requires strstr, but does not include string.h header. I've noticed this in released 3.0.1, but seems to be same on current master. This does not seem to be documented: https://www.openssl.org/docs/manmaster/man3/EVP_EC_gen.html .

I think it should be either mentioned in the documentation or just included in ec.h.
comments: IMO just adding the include to the documentation would be the right fix. Always including it from ec.h seems a little overkill as the ec.h would be used mostly for the legacy EC function calls in existing software and these do not require string.h.
I'm struggling to understand what the purpose of that `strstr` is anyway. Can we just remove it? It looks like a no-op?? Am I missing something? Perhaps @DDvO can shed some light?
Is it some kind of weird way to cast out the const?

> Is it some kind of weird way to cast out the const?

But the underlying `EVP_PKEY_Q_keygen` uses a `va_arg` list anyway...so I would not expect that to make a difference.

I would not have recalled myself why I introduced that weird-looking `strstr(..., "")` call but just found that I mentioned this in https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/14695#discussion_r613131677:
> I added `strstr(curve, "")` in order to provide type checking also for the string variadic arg.

@paulidale liked this and commented:

> Using `strstr(curve, "")` is clever. Another possibly would be `strchr(curve, *curve)`. I don't see much difference between the two, so this isn't a request to change. My initial thought for checking the string type was `curve ""` which doesn't work for pointers so I skipped it. I was in a rush so didn't dwell over other possibilities.

I responded:
> I checked also other possibilities and found that `strstr(curve, "")` is best because, as opposed to alternatives, it is linear in the curve parameter, so macro expansion does not cause problems in case the actual argument filled in for curve has side effects.
I suggest just including string.h and adding a comment explaining why the strstr call is there.

> I suggest just including string.h and adding a comment explaining why the strstr call is there.

Yes, this is what I had in mind, too. Done in #17380.

review_comments:
How about: _strstr is used to enable type checking for the `curve' argument_

The term _variadic string arg_ is kind of non-specific when the macro argument has a name.

What about a separate `char *ossl_check_arg_is_string(char *arg)` function that wraps this for us.

We have similar tricks in the safestack code. E.g. see:

https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/6be83cc655af819be0e3f2701c726a2550357953/include/openssl/safestack.h.in#L37-L65

I'm not sure if its ok to introduce such a trick for 3.0 though.

???? wWhat tricks ????

Inline functions aren't a great solution here since they'll potentially still be instantiated when the macro isn't used.

> ???? wWhat tricks ????

We have inline functions which only have the purpose of checking the type in a macro.

> Inline functions aren't a great solution here since they'll potentially still be instantiated when the macro isn't used.

So?

Given how many problems we've had with inline functions defined in header files, I'm very hesitant to add another one.

The safestack.h functions are part of a macro which only defines them if they are being used.  This is a very significant difference.

> The safestack.h functions are part of a macro which only defines them if they are being used.

This is not the case. They are defined unconditionally. IIRC the problems we had previously were with inline functions that contained references to symbols that weren't then linked. These inline functions have no references to other symbols.

The point was that they produce no code **unless** the macro is used.

This is different to using inline functions here where the function will be defined even if the macro isn't used.
